sections.title: Introduction
rules: Parametric methods assume that data comes from a known probability distribution family.
The density function depends on a fixed set of unknown parameters.
We estimate the parameters from an observed sample of data.
Estimating a few parameters simplifies the learning problem compared to non-parametric density estimation.

sections.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
rules: We assume a sample of independent and identically distributed instances.
The likelihood function is the joint probability density of the observed sample.
The log likelihood function sums the log probabilities of individual observations.
Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameter values that maximize the log likelihood.
For a Bernoulli distribution, the maximum likelihood estimate is the sample mean.
For a Gaussian distribution, the maximum likelihood mean is the sample average.
The maximum likelihood variance is the average squared deviation from the sample mean.

sections.title: Evaluating an Estimator: Bias and Variance
rules: An estimator is a statistic calculated from sample data.
Because the sample is random, the estimator is also a random variable.
The bias of an estimator is the difference between its expected value and the true parameter.
An unbiased estimator has an expected value equal to the true parameter.
The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
The maximum likelihood variance estimator underestimates the true population variance.
Dividing the sum of squared deviations by N minus one yields an unbiased variance estimator.
Variance measures how much the estimator varies across different random samples.
Mean squared error equals the variance plus the squared bias of the estimator.
A consistent estimator converges to the true parameter value as sample size approaches infinity.

sections.title: The Bayes’ Estimator
rules: The Bayesian approach treats unknown parameters as random variables with prior probability distributions.
The prior distribution encodes prior knowledge about parameters before observing data.
Bayes' rule updates the prior distribution into a posterior distribution using the sample likelihood.
The maximum a posteriori estimator chooses the parameter value that maximizes the posterior density.
The Bayes' estimator calculates the expected value of the posterior distribution.
A conjugate prior produces a posterior distribution from the same probability distribution family.
As the sample size increases, the posterior distribution becomes sharper around the maximum likelihood estimate.

sections.title: Parametric Classification
rules: In parametric classification, we model each class-conditional density with a parametric distribution.
When class densities follow Gaussian distributions, each class has a mean and a variance.
Bayes' rule produces the posterior probability for each class.
When classes share equal variances, the quadratic terms cancel and the discriminant function is linear.
When classes have unequal variances, the discriminant function is quadratic.
The decision boundary is the point where the discriminant functions of two classes are equal.

sections.title: Regression
rules: Parametric regression models the dependent variable as a function of the input plus Gaussian noise.
The conditional distribution of the response given the input follows a normal distribution.
Maximizing the log likelihood in regression is mathematically equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared errors.
Linear regression models the output as a linear combination of input features.
We compute optimal regression coefficients by solving the normal equations.
Polynomial regression uses higher-order terms of input features to fit non-linear curves.

sections.title: Tuning Model Complexity: Bias/Variance Dilemma
rules: Expected test error decomposes into bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise.
Bias measures the systematic error caused by incorrect model assumptions.
Variance measures how much the model changes when trained on different datasets.
Simple models have high bias and low variance, causing underfitting.
Complex models have low bias and high variance, causing overfitting.
The optimal model complexity minimizes the sum of squared bias and variance.

sections.title: Model Selection Procedures
rules: Cross-validation estimates generalization error by repeatedly splitting data into training and validation sets.
K-fold cross-validation divides data into K parts, training on K minus one parts.
Leave-one-out cross-validation uses N folds where each fold leaves out one instance.
Regularization adds a penalty term for model complexity to the loss function.
The Akaike Information Criterion penalizes models based on twice the number of free parameters.
The Bayesian Information Criterion applies a stronger penalty based on the logarithm of sample size.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Ronald Fisher introduced the method of maximum likelihood estimation in the nineteen twenties.
Statistical inference provides formal hypothesis tests to compare different parameter estimates.
Balancing bias and variance remains a fundamental challenge across all supervised learning algorithms.
